title: Redwood - Structured Output & Function Calling Demo - Elysium Finance
summary: AE+SE walkthrough of Redwood structured output / JSON mode, function/tool calling with schema enforcement and guardrails; discussed integration options (hosted vs dedicated), data residency and KMS, and Optimize recommendations for batching and quantization. Agreed to run a benchmark POC and share security/compliance docs.

Priya to share structured-output demo notebook and schema examples (link)
Elysium to provide 1 month of example prompts and data distribution
Schedule POC baseline benchmark run (week of 2026-05-04)

transcript: Meeting Header: 2026-04-21 15:00 PDT | Duration: 47 mins | Location: Zoom | Recording: Yes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Sam O'Neill (Redwood SE) — Markus Chen (Elysium CTO), Aisha Patel (Head of ML), David Ruiz (Infra), Sofia Gomez (Product)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining; we'll keep this to ~45 minutes, run through structured output and function calling in Redwood, and leave time for questions — Priya will demo the console and API flows.

[00:18] Markus: Sounds good, thanks. we're mainly concerned about reliably returning JSON for our downstream pipeline, and preventing hallucinated fields — and we need to see how function calling works for actioning trades in our sandbox, not real money yet.

[00:33] Priya: totally. quick overview: Redwood's JSON mode plus schema enforcement means you can give a JSON schema, and the model is constrained to emit that shape; we also add soft and hard guardrails — the soft is a post-hoc validator suggestion, hard rejects outputs that don't match and you can route to fallback model or error handling.
[00:50] Aisha: when you say 'hard', do you actually drop the response or do you try to repair it? we have workflows that prefer a best-effort repair rather than hard failures.

[01:05] Priya: great question — it's configurable. repair attempts are offered by Redwood Optimize; we run a small in-proc schema fixer that attempts to coerce types or fill missing fields using the model with context, and if that fails we can return structured error codes. that behavior is a policy toggle per route.

[01:28] Sam: demo note: we'll show two paths — API-first (curl/SDK) and Console where you can generate schemas from examples and test with synthetic traffic; plus we'll show a function-calling flow that triggers a mocked 'execute_trade' tool via the tool-calling shim.
[01:47] Sofia: and security? we can't have keys leaving our VPC for the POC — is dedicated or private required?

[02:00] Jordan: for POCs we often start on Hosted with strict network egress rules, but for Elysium's security posture Dedicated or Private deployment is typical. we'll cover KMS and audit logs in the security doc we send after this call.
[02:18] Markus: ok, please include SOC2 scope and whether logs can go to our SIEM.
[02:30] Priya: yes — we have event-level audit logs and can forward via syslog or an S3/GCS sink depending on deployment. notes on SIEM and audit retention will be in the security packet.
[02:46] Jordan: Priya, take it away on the demo.

[03:00] [Screen share starts] Priya: opening the Redwood Console — Projects > Elysium-POC. here's the Structured Output tab. first, I paste a JSON schema for a trade recommendation (symbol:string, side: enum, size:number, confidence:number between 0-1, metadata object).

[03:25] [03:25] Priya (demo): I'm toggling 'strict_validation: true' and 'repair_attempts: 2' in the route config. note: we also can set 'fallback_model: gpt-neox-variant' to drop to a cheaper emergent model if strict fails.
[03:46] David: is 'fallback_model' compatible with kv-cache and latency SLOs? we can't have huge latency spikes in production.

[04:00] Sam: fallback is subject to routing latency policy; you can set max-allowed-latency and Redwood will either queue or return an error. we surface token-level latency breakdowns in Console so you can see the hit from falling back.

[04:18] [04:18] Priya: switching to API demo — curl example: POST /v1/generate with 'mode: json' and 'schema: <schema json>'. here's the SDK snippet in python. we call the model, and Redwood returns 'output' plus 'structured_output' object and 'validation' metadata.
[04:44] [04:44] Transcript artifact: shared link to demo notebook and schema examples: https://redwood.com/demos/structured-output-notebook (note: internal link)

[05:00] [05:00] Priya: i'll send the notebook after. now function/tool calling: we register a tool called 'execute_trade' in the route config — a schema for the tool input is enforced, and the runtime will only call that tool when the parsed structured output includes an 'action' field with action.type == 'execute_trade'.
[05:26] Aisha: so is that like OpenAI function calling where model decides to call the function? we want to control when it's allowed to call external systems.

[05:38] Priya: it's similar but with additional policy layers — you can whitelist which tools a model variant can call, require manual approval for first N calls, or put the call into a safelist. there's also an approval webhook for human-in-the-loop flows.
[05:59] Markus: can we map that to our IAM? e.g., only certain service accounts can anoint a tool to execute?
[06:12] Sam: yes — RBAC ties into tools; in Private/Dedicated we can map tool execution to customer service accounts, and audit each call with correlation IDs for your SIEM.

[06:28] [06:28] Priya: demo: I'm running a sample prompt 'Recommend trades based on overnight flow and risk budget 2%' — hitting the API. here's the raw response: sometimes the model proposes an extra field like 'est_pct' instead of 'size' — with schema enforcement we catch that and either coerce or return a structured error.
[06:53] [06:53] Transcript note: imperfect transcription — 'KV cache' heard as 'KV cash' in places, occasional mis-said proper nouns like 'GCP' -> 'G C P' etc.

[07:10] Priya: example of a failed match: the model returned side: 'buy-ish' — but enum only allows 'buy' or 'sell'. Repair attempt invoked and transformer prompt asked the model to normalize to 'buy' with justification; if repair confidence < threshold, it emits validation_error with code VAL_01.
[07:36] Aisha: what's the performance hit for repair attempts? we care about p99 latency.

[07:45] Sam: repair is a short model call and is charged as incremental tokens; Optimize can recommend when to enable repair based on trade-off curves — for low-latency we suggest enabling repair only for background or batch flows and prefer strict reject for latency-critical sync paths.

[08:03] [08:03] Priya: switching to the Optimize tab — here we have recommendations: batching thresholds, quantization profile suggestions per model, and a suggested runtime config: for our trade workload we recommend 8-token warmup, KV cache enabled, batch target 16, and a quant 4-bit profile on 80% of requests for non-critical streams.
[08:30] David: quantify the cost delta — ballpark?
[08:36] Priya: using sample load, Optimize predicts ~35% token-cost savings with the quant profile and batching; we'd run a short benchmark to validate with your prompt set — that's part of the POC.
[08:50] Markus: about data residency — we need EU-only for certain customers. can you pin region?
[08:56] Jordan: yes, route-level region pinning and private deployments allow region-restricted inference. we'll include region mapping in the POC template.

[09:10] [09:10] Priya: back to function calling: here's a trace view in Console — you can see model_fingerprint, which model variant served, validation result, and tool_call_payload (masked by default). we support redaction and token-level masking for PII.
[09:32] Aisha: masking by default is good; can we bring our PII classifier to the pipeline?
[09:40] Sam: you can plug in a pre-processing webhook or use the Redwood prefilter that integrates custom regexes or classifier endpoints before the model sees prompts.

[09:55] [09:55] Priya: now i'll demo the function call — i'm toggling sandbox_execution:true, the tool is stubbed to return a success payload. watch the transcript: model returns structured_output with action:{type:'execute_trade', payload:{symbol:'XYZ', side:'sell', size:120}} and Redwood runtime invokes the stubbed tool and returns tool_response in the call.
[10:25] [10:25] (audio: multiple people chuckle) Markus: that was clean — but how do we handle idempotency and replay?

[10:35] Priya: every tool call gets a stable request_id and we annotate with idempotency keys you provide or we generate. we also keep a call history for audit and can enforce one-time-only via the tool adapter.
[10:48] David: for the private deployment — does the tool adapter run in our network or in Redwood's runtime?

[10:56] Sam: in Private, tool adapters can run inside your VPC as sidecars; in Hosted, adapters are in our control plane but you can configure strict egress policies or use webhooks into your network via private endpoints.

[11:14] [11:14] Priya: moving on — error modes. we surfaced a few error classes: validation_error, policy_block (e.g., guardrail hit), tool_exec_error. each has recommended handling patterns in our docs.
[11:34] Aisha: policy_block — can we see an example?

[11:40] Priya: yes: if the model tries to call an off-limits tool or produce PII in a restricted field, the route policy will return policy_block with code POL_403 and a human-readable reason. you can also configure silent-drop for denied actions.

[11:58] [11:58] Jordan: redwood note: our sample security artifact link: https://redwood.com/security/elysium-poc-pack.pdf — we'll share post-call and it includes SOC2, ISO, KMS integrations, and audit log samples.
[12:16] Markus: good — please include whether HSM-backed keys are supported for private.
[12:24] Jordan: yes HSM/KMS supported; we'll include the exact vendors and certs in the packet.

[12:35] [12:35] Priya: quick dev flow: you push a schema, we version it, and you can pin a model+schema pair. rollouts support canary (5/20/100) and automatic fallback if validation regresses based on your eval set.
[12:56] Aisha: how do we run evals?
[13:00] Priya: Console has an Evals tab where you upload prompt-output pairs and we run regression checks across models and quantization profiles; you get diff metrics and flagged regressions.
[13:18] [13:18] Transcript: slight stutter by speaker — 'quanization' instead of 'quantization' appears in the audio, corrected in notes.
[13:28] David: networking — for Dedicated, do we use private peering?
[13:33] Sam: Dedicated supports cloud peering and private links; Private deployment gives you full on-prem control but has longer lead times.
[13:46] Markus: timeline for POC? we want baseline in two weeks and a follow-up by end of May.
[13:54] Jordan: proposed: baseline benchmark week of May 4, 1-week POC to run: profiling + evals, checkpoint call May 11. we'll send calendar invites after this call.

[14:08] [14:08] Priya: live API trace example — showing validation metadata: is_valid:false, errors:[{field:'side', issue:'enum_mismatch', raw_value:'buy-ish'}], repair_attempts:1, repaired_value:'buy', repair_confidence:0.94 — traces are stored and searchable.
[14:40] Aisha: are traces sampled? storing every token trace would be huge.
[14:46] Priya: traces are sampled by default and configurable; you can keep 100% traces for flagged requests and enable longer retention for audit routes.

[15:00] [15:00] Demo: switched to SDK quickstart — python example showing how to provide a schema as a dictionary, call client.generate, check response['structured_output'], and conditionally call tools via client.invoke_tool.
[15:22] Markus: any SDKs for Java/Go?
[15:26] Jordan: yes — we have official SDKs for Python, Node, Java, and a gRPC interface for high-throughput services.
[15:37] Sofia: ok let's talk about pricing model for Dedicated — we need committed capacity but also burstable for earnings spikes.
[15:46] Jordan: Dedicated has reserved GPU pools with burst credits; we'll include a sizing sheet and cost model in the pricing doc. contract can include burst protections and SLO credits.
[16:00] [16:00] Priya: one more advanced bit: conditional output routing — you can set rules so that high-confidence predictions go to execute_tool, medium to dry-run queue, low to human review.
[16:18] Aisha: human review UI?
[16:22] Sam: Console offers a review queue with diffs and suggested edits; integrates with Slack/Teams for approvals.
[16:35] [16:35] Markus: regulatory: can Redwood support long-term retention controls and redaction for EU regs?
[16:44] Jordan: yes — retention policies by route, PII redaction, and region pinning. we'll send policy examples.

[16:57] [16:57] Priya: running a small live synthetic load to demo latency — hitting 200 qps with batch target 16; console shows p50/p95/p99 — p99 is ~220ms in this synthetic setup with KV cache warmed.
[17:18] David: realistic load for us will be 1k qps peak, but many are background — what's recommended architecture?

[17:28] Sam: for that scale we'd suggest Dedicated with autoscaling GPU pools, sharded KV caches, and separate route tiers for sync vs async. Optimize can suggest slot counts based on your latency SLO and token distribution.
[17:46] Aisha: are model weights or cache persisted across restarts?
[17:52] Priya: KV cache is persisted warm for active shards; model weights are managed by runtime and have warmup heuristics; Optimize suggests warmup token counts per route.
[18:05] [18:05] Jordan: ok we're coming up on time — quick recap and next actions.

[18:12] Jordan: Recap: 1) Redwood will send POC pricing + contract 2) Priya will share demo notebook, schema examples, and sample API snippets 3) Elysium to provide prompts and network/KMS details 4) baseline benchmark week of May 4 — Jordan to send invites.
[18:33] Markus: sounds good. one more ask — can you include a sample of the 'repair' prompt used so we can vet justification text for compliance?
[18:42] Priya: yes we'll include the repair prompt template and an example of the repair justification output.
[18:50] Sofia: also, include runbook for policy_block handling so our SREs know how to detect and triage.
[18:58] Jordan: will do.
[19:05] [19:05] Final quick Q&A: Aisha: any blockers you see? Priya: none immediate; need sample prompts and infra details. Jordan: we'll follow up with required docs by 2026-04-24.
[19:23] Jordan: thanks everyone, talk soon — demo recording and artifacts will be shared.
[19:30] Meeting end.
Notes: timestamps approximate; transcript retains spoken disfluencies; some proper nouns may be mis-transcribed.
